newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Drnovsek triumphs to lead Slovenian government.
newsitem.headline: Drnovsek triumphs to lead Slovenian government.

text.p: Janez Drnovsek triumphed in a parliamentary vote on Thursday to lead a new Slovenian government, ending two months of political deadlock after inconclusive general elections.

In a knife-edge vote, parliament backed the centre-left Liberal Democrat leader, prime minister for the past four years, by 46 votes to 44 after an acrimonious two-day debate laced with accusations of dirty deals and corruption.
"Before us is a very demanding path. We need to form a government, we need to ensure Slovenia's political stability," Drnovsek told parliament after the result was announced.

Parliament had been split evenly between Drnovsek's party and its allies and a rightwing bloc until a member of the rightwing Christian Democrats defected from his party on Wednesday to support Drnovsek.
The Liberal Democrats won 25 of 90 parliamentary seats in the November 10 general election, Slovenia's second since independence from Yugoslavia in 1991.

In weeks of negotiations, the Liberal Democrats won the support of smaller parties in parliament, including former communists, but clinching the one extra vote needed for an absolute majority appeared remote until Wednesday's surprise defection by Ciril Pucko.

Pucko, whose family have been given police protection since his decision to leave the Christian Democrats, defended his decision by saying Slovenia needed a government as soon as possible to avoid instability.

His defection infuriated the rightwing alliance, consisting of the conservative People's Party, the centre-right Social Democrats and the Christian Democrats, which had been confident of defeating Drnovsek to shift Slovenian politics to the right.

People's Party leader Marjan Podobnik, who leads the so-called "Spring" alliance and had been tipped as a potential prime minister, said any charges of corruption against the Liberal Democrats had to be cleared.

"I hope the 46th vote was found on the basis of political persuasion," a dejected-looking Podobnik told Slovenian television. "We had wished Slovenia would get a quality government but after the past two days I am less convinced that is possible."

His political ally, Social Democrat leader Janez Jansa, said Drnovsek had no chance of forming a stable administration and was more forthright in accusing the Liberal Democrats of behind-the-scenes deals.
"The vote clearly showed that power can be retained by political corruption," he told reporters.
Despite the charges, Drnovsek and his party could breathe a sigh of relief that the ordeal was over. He has to present his government lineup before parliament within 15 days.

With the support of leftists, Drnovsek may have a hard time to bring in tough economic reform, including necessary spending cuts, if he wants to achieve his goal of preparing Slovenia for European Union membership by the year 2001.

But Drnovsek won praise abroad during his first term of office for creating a stable democracy and one of the most thriving economies among Europe's ex-communist states while other former Yugoslav states went to war.
